title: Overdue
paragraphs: We found it while clearing Atok’s wardrobe, three weeks after the funeral: a hardcover book in a brown-paper jacket, tucked beneath his folded sarongs as if it were something precious or something shameful. Inside the cover was a paper pocket and a slip of stamped dates. The last stamp, in violet ink gone pale with age, said 14 MAR 1979.

“More than forty years overdue,” my mother said, and laughed, and then stopped laughing and had to sit down on the bed. The book was a guide to shore birds, with painted plates. Atok had put neat pencil ticks beside some of them — the kingfisher, the little heron, the sandpiper — and beside each tick a place and a date. The last tick was from only two years ago, in handwriting that shook.

“Take it back,” my mother told me. “He hated owing people.” I did not want to. I worked out the fine on my phone, at so many cents a day, and got a number that made my stomach drop. More than that, I did not want to hand the ticks to a stranger behind a counter. But my mother had the look of someone holding herself together with clothes pegs, so on Saturday I took the book on the bus, in a plastic bag on my lap, like a pot of something that might spill.

The library was nothing Atok would have recognised. Glass doors breathed open by themselves. Machines swallowed returned books through a slot and blinked green. I stood before one of them for a long time. The slot was the width of a letterbox and just as final. A small boy behind me sighed loudly, the way people do when they want you to know they are being patient.

I stepped out of the queue and went to the desk instead. The librarian was a tall man with reading glasses pushed up into grey hair. I had my explanation ready — my grandfather, the wardrobe, I can pay a bit every month — but it came out backwards and tangled, and in the end I simply slid the book across. He opened it at the date slip. He was quiet for so long that I began counting the ceiling lights.

“Nineteen seventy-nine,” he said at last, almost fondly. “This branch wasn’t even built. It would have come from the old place by the river, the one with the fans that never worked.” He turned the pages slowly and stopped at a tick. “Your grandfather saw a blue-eared kingfisher at the reservoir? I’ve been trying to see one for eleven years.” He did not sound like a man about to mention money.

“The fine—” I began. He tapped at his keyboard, frowned, tapped again. “This title was written off before I was hired. As far as our records are concerned, it doesn’t exist.” He closed the cover with two hands, the way you close a door on a sleeping child. “I can’t fine a book that doesn’t exist. I can’t put one on a shelf, either.” He pushed it back across the desk. “I think it had better stay lost.”

I carried the book home on my lap again, more carefully than before. That evening my mother found me at the window with it open, squinting at a brown bird on the railing of the opposite block. I had a pencil. It was an ordinary mynah, I am fairly sure, and it flew off before I could decide; but I had already turned to the back, where there was a clean page, and written the date.

scheme.answer: Atok may have hidden it because he treasured it [1], or because he was embarrassed at never having returned it [1].
points: He valued / treasured the book greatly.
He was embarrassed / felt guilty about it (about having kept it).

seeds.text: His grandfather may have hidden it because he treasured the book very much, or because he was embarrassed that he had never returned it.

points: First she found it funny that the book was so many years late.
Then the book reminded her of her father / of his death, and her grief overcame her.

seeds.text: At first she found it funny that the book was so many years late. Then it reminded her that her father was gone and she was overcome by grief.
